div1.head: Interview with Jane A. La Mar [4/6/2004]

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: This is Caroline Mitchell. I'm an attorney with the law firm Jones Day in San Francisco, California. It's April 6, 2004. We are recording an interview of Jane La Mar for the Veterans History Project. The people present at the interview are myself, Jane La Mar and operating the video equipment David Mendella, Jane's daughter Jamie Malone and her daughter Katie. If you could begin by talking about the first time that you thought about learning how to fly.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: All right. I guess I never thought about it. My -- my day and the stock I came from, we weren't rich, and I thought you had to be rich, and it wasn't until I was working for my uncle who had a print shop, and he hired a young man, we were about the same age, and we got acquainted, and he said he just soloed and would I like to go out and take a ride? Well, that sounded fun to me, so we went to Alhambra Airport in those days, and he arranged for me to take a ride in an airplane. It was a biplane, two places in the front, the pilot sat in the back, and that gave me my first ride.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And approximately when was that?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: About -- oh, early 1936.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And how old were you?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: I was, oh, gee, 20. And so I had gone to -- to junior high for a while, but I just -- I just didn't like school. I'm not a scholar. I love to read, but I don't want to be told what to read. So I was working for my uncle in the depression days, and so when Bill asked me if I wanted to take a ride in the airplane, I just thought -- you know, thought fine. So I loved it, and the next week I started taking lessons. That's about what happened.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And so was it very expensive to take lessons then?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Well, everything is relative, of course, but when you made as much as 15 dollars a week on a good week, it cost me 8 dollars an hour to fly, I didn't do much flying, but I loved the atmosphere. I loved being with the people that were learning to fly, and as it happened, I was the first girl student this instructor had, and so eventually, there were two other girls, and that was about -- you know, it's about 100 to one today women learning to fly. I So I would hang around the airport all day, and then just before it got too dark to fly, I would take my 15 or 20 minutes. That was about -- about -- I would get .- oh, maybe, once, twice a week I'd fly for 20 minutes.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: That's great. Now, who -- can you tell us a little bit about your instructor.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Oh, yes. Of course, I think everybody gets a crush on their instructor, but Jim had -- I don't know when he learned to fly. It must have been not long before I did because that's the way things work, but he became -- eventually, he became a examiner for the FAA and eventually, I think, the top man in Southern California until he finally retired years and years later, but those -- well, I don't know, it just -- I just don't know how much to get into any of this, so you better ask me questions.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Yeah. Okay. And so what was Jim's full name?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Jim -- Alfred James Dooey, so his name is Jim Dooey. His father was a fairly well-known artist in those days, too.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Oh, that's interesting. And what kind of plane -- did he only have one I plane when you started learning to fly?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Yes, he had just one airplane. It was called a Dehavilland Gypsy Moth, and it was a biplane, and it's funny, it was built I think about 1929, so really wasn't that old an airplane, and eventually, the Gypsy Moth with war power and very little change became the primary airplane for teaching people in Canada and Great Britain, and it just went on and on, it seemed like, but it's -- it's the one I soloed, and I soloed in about six hours, ten minutes, I think my logbook says, and I soloed in 1936. So I - I mean, I just took to flying. It was just like something naturally, and I could do it, and I never even thought about it.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm. And then did you eventually get a different kind of plane?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Oh, yes, I went through two or three airplanes, like pilots did with their own air bases or own flying services, and the -- the time I bought the Ryan STA, that was like --like somebody buying a Ferrari today. It was a low wing monoplane. It had -- instead of the round radial engine most airplanes have, it had an in-line engine like cars have, and it was absolutely beautiful. I fell in love with it, and I that's the only thing I flew almost, I mean the only thing I paid to fly from then on the rest of my life.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And then did you -- did you have to learn everything about how the planes worked and --

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Well, I only did that much later.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: I think when I frrst learned to fly, I had to have some kind of a small test just to pass the -- the private license, but I can't remember there was anything very complicated about it because there wasn't that much to learn in those days. Airplanes didn't have any electrical system, no radio. The engine was taken care of by somebody else. I didn't have to learn to do that, but eventually, I had to learn a lot about it when I went on in my flying.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And what kind -- what did you wear when you went flying?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Just slacks, shirt just like girls would wear today, nothing fancy.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And did you have to wear goggles or something? I

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Oh, yeah, you had to have a helmet and goggles because an open airplane, you would just blow away if you didn't.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Yeah, yeah.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: That's the only thing that made you look different, you could go around wearing a helmet and goggles.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And what kind of -- where were you flying when you were flying?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Well, I was at the Alhambra Airport--

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: -- the first flying I did, and I -- from then on, well, I just had moved on to Southern California to Virginia to wherever.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm. And then so you soloed, and then did you get your license after that?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Yeah, I did, but with 20 minutes or so a time, it took me two years to have the 35 hours I had to have to apply for a license, and so the time finally came, and I flew down to Mines Field -- you know Mines Field is Los Angeles International these days --

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Oh, okay.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: -- and took -- I need some water. My bottle is right there; makes me thirsty.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Ob, I bet.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Thank you. Just hold everything. Ready again?

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Okay. Mines Field in those days was just a -- a dirt field. It had -- had a few buildings on it, but it was nothing out of the ordinary at all. I don't even remember there being a tower. If it was, I didn't have radio, so I didn't use it. If they had to flash lights at me, that I don't remember. What I do remember was after I met the man that did the flight test for me, I flew for a little while, I think, with him, and then he got out. He said well, go fly over those hills at a certain altitude and do the spins. In those days, you had to demonstrate a spin. You had to go, I think, one-and a half to the left and one and a half to the right.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: But he wasn't going to ride with me, and I'm not the first one, I've read this I from other women, but I took off again. I went up over the hills. I did the required spins, came back, landed, and that was a spot landing. You weren't supposed to use the engine at all, supposed to cut the throttle, come down, approach the airport, make a landing in a certain spot, and then he got back in, and we flew some more. Well, I passed, and that was fine. That was a real thrill.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Oh, I bet that was exciting.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Mines Field was a thrill.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hrnm, that's great. Now, what did your mother think of you learning to fly, doing all this?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: We never really talked about it. She said if I wanted to, that's fine, just be careful.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hrnm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: It was 30 years before she ever flew with me.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Oh, is that right? Now, did you meet your husband in this whole process?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Well, in a way, but after the Alhambra days, Jim Dooey moved to a little airport called Telegraph on Atlantic. It's right off the two main roads in Los Angeles. I think towards -- sort of the southeast. Anyway, Telegraph and Atlantic --

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: -- and I had -- I wasn't doing much flying in those days, but I had gone in the airport just to get acquainted again, and they had formed a flying club among the fellas, and as initiation, they had to make a parachute jump.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: So some young guy was going to do the jump that day, so I got in a car with another couple fellas, and we went over to pick him up. Well, when Sam landed and we brought him home, that was the start of a beautiful friendship, but that's how I met him.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And so then around what time was that?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: That had to be probably early 1940 'cause we were married in November 23, 1940. So about -- after about six months, I remember.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Okay. And then what happened next in your flying career after that?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Well, okay. After we were married and we were living in Tujunga, Sam was working for Lockheed as a junior engineer, and so war came along, changed everything. There was no flying done in -- anywhere along the coast. You had to go back inland a couple hundred miles, and so I just -- I was just sitting out the war, so to speak, and I think in the first place, I've always hesitated doing this because I've always felt guilty because I enjoyed the war so much, and that's an awful thing to say now, but my family never got hurt by it.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm. .

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: And two cousins, one was a Navy pilot, the other was a Army pilot, had a cousin that went into the South Seas in the Army. He ended up on a desk for the whole time, and so living where I did in Rialto in those days family -- everything seems so far away, and yet I -- I served as a lookout once because everybody took their turn doing that, watched for strange airplanes.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And where did you do that?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Where did you do that?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: In Rialto. They had watch towers set up all over Southern -- well, all over the states, I'm sure, anywhere close to where the Japanese might come in, which was absurd, but anyway, I did that for a while. I took a first aid course that everybody took. We -- that kind of stuff I could do, but it wasn't until again through Jim Dooey I had a chance to -- to kind of go back to flight school to become a instructor, got a commercial license, I got my instructor's rating, and by -- by getting that, now I had a real profession. The government had set up this school, and it was in Fresno, and it was to teach fairly experienced pilots how to be instructors because in those days, after the war, CPT, the Civilian Pilot Training program, changed to a War Training Service program. Women weren't allowed to belong anymore. No woman learned to fly in WTS, but they needed instructors, and a woman instructor is fine. So I did that, and to -- to pay for the - my flying, I had to contract to teach at least one WTS program.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And what does WTS mean, do you--

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: War Training Service.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: And so again, most -- all the other pilot training schools in California were like -- were taught by mostly men. They had two or three women, but the regular, the smaller schools all were, oh, couple hundred miles east, and I didn't want to be out on the desert. So I had a chance to go to Ridgefield, Utah, of all things, and I got my first taste of instructing there. It was -- it was fun.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And who did you instruct?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Okay. I had what I called pre-pre-Navy cadets because they were given a taste of flying. They were given the equivalent of a private license, 35 hours, and then when they finished, if they were good enough to do that, then they went on to become real pilots, other flying schools. And so I had four young guys, probably not a whole lot younger than myself, and they were all from Long Beach, and first time really that I flew in a Piper Cub because I had, oh, two or three rides, but I'd always kinda, I I suppose, looked down on a Piper Cub, but a great little airplane for just training other people to fly, and they're still flying 'em in air shows all over the place.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And what did the men that you had as students think of having a woman instructor?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Oh, they didn't seem to mind. I never heard anybody object, and I -- I was told I did a good job, and I - was lucky to have -- well, the -- the people I worked with were nice people, and I had one man who -- an old-time instructor sorta, so I could ask him questions, and I read the book, and I'd reread the book, and my only problem, I had one young fella that got sick every time we flew.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Oh, is that right?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: That was terrible, yeah, and luckily, in the Cub I sat in the front, he sat in back of me, and the cub has a wide door that's hinged so the top can go up and the bottom go down. You have all this wide space in between. So I never got hit by anything, but he always had to clean the airplane when we got home.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: And I had read that if your I student gets sick, it's your fault, you should clean the airplane. Well, they didn't make me do that. That was his job.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Yeah, that makes sense. Now, were there other women instructors at the same place or were you the only one?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: No, I was the only one.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And how long were you there for?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: It was about two months, I think, before they fInished their -- their flying and military training and the ground school that they also got there, and then a Thompson Flying Service was out of Salt Lake City, and they notifIed me they were going to change the program a little bit and I wouldn't be needed anymore. I don't think it was because I didn't do a good job. I think they honestly changed the program.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: And so anyway, it gave me freedom to go back home again, and I -- I went back to Rialto. Sam had been classified, I think it was lA, somebody that was important enough in what they were doing that they weren't drafted.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: And -- and so I had heard about the -- sorry, the WASPS for years, ever since the war started, but in the beginning, the first time I ever heard of 'em, they required 500 hours. Well, there weren't a hundred women in the United States at that time 1940 that had 500 hours.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: So I put that aside, and then I went ahead and got the instructor's rating. I built up flying time. Gradually, the amount of time needed to apply for the WASPS came down till all of a sudden it was 30 hours, and I just couldn't believe it. Anyway, I applied. So Jacquelyn Cochran was running the WASPS by then.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And could you explain for a minute what the WASP was?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Oh, it's -- I think it was Women Army -- 'cause it wasn't Air Force, Women's Army Service Pilots.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: And the -- they had their own field back in Sweetwater, Texas, and had been an airport, air base for training British pilots, I and we were training British fellas to fly over here, and so she was able to -- to get the release of that airport, and so we had our own field, our own instructors, our own airplanes. In fact, it was the only airport in the whole United States that devoted entirely to women.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: And so when I finally got there, I had to take an interview by some -- one of Cochran's associates. I had to go to Marshfield which is by -- closest place to take a physical that was identical as to the physicals that men got. And so I finally got all -- everything I had to do, and so I sat and waited, and I wrote and I said I'm ready to go. If you have a cancellation, I'll come. Well, didn't do any good. I finally got word to report to Sweetwater in probably September, '41, it had to be, and so Sam got -- we had a good excuse. Trains were crowded with military troops, the buses were crowded, and no airplanes were flying that way. I mean, that was all military. So he got permission to drive me to Sweetwater, Texas, and it was fun. We had a wonderful trip, stopped by Carlsbad caverns on the way and finally got to Sweetwater and said my good-byes, climbed in the bus with all the other girls and started my military training there.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: It was something I'd wanted to do all my life.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: That's great. Now, so what was the training like?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: It was fun. Now, remember, I already had an instructor's rating. I had already flown the primary trainer that we were assigned to, had over 60 hours in it.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: So the primary was -- was a piece of cake, so they say. I was one of the first ones to solo with -- another girl in another class soloed the same day, and Sweetwater, the one who soloed first got thrown in the wishing well.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Oh, my.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: At the beginning -- at the front of the administration building for Avenger Field, that's what it was called, Avenger, was a fountain, and that was called a wishing well. You could toss some pennies into it before you had your check ride and all that. So anyway, we got doused. Now, there -- we still didn't really have uniforms at that time. We wore what we call zoot suits. They were actually just coveralls and the smallest that the Army had for girls, so we kind of buckled 'em up tight and rolled up the sleeves and rolled up the legs, and that was our everyday uniform, and then we all had just khaki tan pants, white blouses, and that was our uniform, and, of course, we were issued the flying jackets that every Army airport pilot flew -- flew in, sorry, the jackets that still people buy today that look like, and we were issued winter flying clothes, heavy fleece-lined pants and coats and, of course, goggles. I had my own goggles, but they had goggles; they had helmets. I think everything else was issued to us.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And so then what happened after you soloed?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Oh, we kept on -- just usual training, the things people learn as -- to go on through flying. I can't remember, there was -- you just -- you were graduated from primary into secondary--

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: -- and the secondary planes were the bigger ones. They were like 400 -- 450 horsepower airplanes. They had a lot of power. The fust ones, the basics, weren't retractable gear, but they were -- they were most -- the biggest planes I'd flown up to that time, and then when we got through that phase, I went into the AT -6's, the North American Texan --

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hrmn.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: -- which is still flown today at air shows, and it was -- actually, the AT -6 was a final step before the military pilot climbed into the p51 's, the pursuit airplanes, the P-47's, the class of the flying world.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Wow. And then so what happened, what did you do after you finished in Texas? Did you end up going home or--

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Well, no, after -- I -- I kind - I don't know, I -- what happened really. In fact, I didn't get in when I wanted to. The fact that war was coming to an end, I just decided time to go home --

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hrmn.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: -- so I did. I got a ride back to San Diego, and Sam came down and picked me up, and there on I just kinda set out, wait for the war to end.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm. And did it end pretty shortly after that?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Yeah. Well, not -- not really. It didn't end till '45.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: But it ended for me anyway.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm. And then did you continue flying after the war?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: No, I didn't. After I got home, just still those years where nobody could fly--

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: -- and then I decided, having come home, I knew I wasn't going to do anything in the military anymore, I decided it was time to be a good wife, raise a family and get into that part of my life, and that's what I did. That's when Jamie was born in '45, and my younger daughter in '48, and I didn't get back into flying until '5 -- it was '58. Sam had bought a little airplane called a Taylorcraft, a little two place fabric high wing airplane with about 65 horsepower engine, no radio, and he thought he could commute to Long Beach. By that time, he was working for Douglas and trying to drive back and forth, which was about 75 mile per hour -- 75-mile drive.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: So anyway, he bought the airplane, 1,000 dollars, and it didn't work out to commute, but it got me back into flying again 'cause in '58, I renewed my instructor's rating, and I just started flying wherever I could, flying club in Manning, a flying club in Redland, a flying club in Riverside.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Somebody who wanted to learn to fly knew I'd instructed, and so I just picked up time here and there, and it was fun; you know, people were paying me to do something I paid for.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: -- and you can't beat that.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: It was great.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And then what happened eventually with your flying career?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Well, flying around with different people, I had become acquainted with one of the businessmen in town, an electrical engineer, and he -- he was a pilot, too. He had a 16-year-old daughter. Well, the 16-year-old daughter's boyfriend moved back to Delaware, or close to Delaware somewhere, but anyway, East Coast, and she wanted to go visit him. Well, she and her father cooked up the idea that if I would be the pilot, he would pay for the - the - the cost for the Powder Puff Derby--

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Oh.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: - and so gee, you know, I...that sounded pretty neat. Nobody'd ever offered that before. I even hardly knew what the Powder Puff Derby was. I just knew it was an all women's air race that went from the West Coast to the East Coast and had to be a load of fun. Well, Alec -- Alex Ferguson, Alec owned a Cessna 182 which was a pretty nice airplane in those days, high wing, 200 some power airplane and held four people. So because Alec was a top businessman in town, the mayor was our doctor, the police chief I'd known since we moved to Rialto, and the whole town got behind it and sponsored the -- me for the Powder Puff Derby.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Oh, that's great.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: We - it was fun. I've still got clippings. The airplane was flown in. They didn't let me do it, but I could have. It was easy, they just walked off a straight street a mile long. An ex Air Force pilot actually did the flying, and so we landed there. We taxied into town. The airplane was parked right in front of the city hall. They'd had a professional painter paint the Rialto bridge, you know, from the Italian -- from Venice --

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: -- the Rialto bridge over the canal. Anyway, that was painted on the side of the airplane, and so I had -- I mean, I was I was a big frog in a little puddle in those days. So we -- the takeoff was actually down in Torrance Airport, and the whole town went, seemed like, went down to see me off. We had the mayor again, the police chief and Alex all went down to see us off, and so we got in the airplane, took off and we headed to Atlantic City where we had actually landed. Well, we made it; we didn't get lost; we didn't have any problem. There's always two or three pilots every year that get lost, it seems like, and, of course, there were 100 airplanes, I think, that year. It got awfully big, just more and more people were starting to fly in it. And so when we got there, Kathy, my little copilot, went off with her boyfriend's family, and we had arranged that if I was going to be there with a whole airplane to bring home empty, then Jamie and Vicky ought to go back to see their cousins in Syracuse, New York, and I would pick up everybody and fly us all home. Well, it worked out -- it worked out beautifully. I mean, we went into New York. I can remember riding the taxi cabs 'cause I wouldn't get on a subrail. I was scared of a subway. So taxi drivers were supposed to be rude, unpleasant. Well, I didn't find it so. I thought - they took pity on me, I guess, me and my two little girls. So we rode the taxi whenever we went out of the hotel, and then Sam met us, and we had to go out to -- oh, Teterborough (sic), I believe it was, to pick up our airplane again. I'd flown it up there after the race. I didn't -- I was only 50 something in the race, but -- then we had -- we got to fly up to Syracuse, New York, where -- and pick up Jamie and Becky, and we I started home just across the country, and if you want a nice way to see lots -- see the United States, you see it from the air about 3,500 feet high, not 35,000.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Right.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: It was just a wonderful trip home. We stopped at Cleveland, saw Sam's older sister, and then I can remember getting to Cheyenne and how I loved the smell of the sage brush in Cheyenne and gradually got home, got us all safely home.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm. And so did you participate in the Powder Puffs after that?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Oh, definitely, I got hooked, not as much as some people, but I did fly again the next year. I flew it -- skipped a year, I think. When we moved back to Virginia, the flying service back there offered to sponsor me in the Powder Puff Derby, so I called up a friend I'd taught to fly in Rialto, and so she met me. We took off, I think from -- oh, jeepers, I forget, San Diego, can't remember, and so again, we don't win. I never did come anywhere close to winning, but we had a lot of fun, and we got back to Manasses safe and sound. She took a flight home I with some other western girl who had to fly home, so she got home safely, and then I didn't fly again until -- not in the derby, I mean, back I guess it was '60 -- came back '66, probably in '66 I flew it again --

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: -- and I flew it several more times.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: And then can you tell us about your career with the FAA?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Oh, yeah. Yeah, that was pretty nice. I - I kept moving. I mean, I -- eventually back in Virginia I decided I didn't belong there, so I came back to California, and and from Riverside, I moved up to Redding, California, and in Redding, I - I was lucky enough to find a job instructing with a little airport on the south side of town who had a real wheeler dealer for a owner. Anyway, John O'Brien had spoken to the FAA to see if he could get me on as an examiner because his little flying school, his little flying operation, if he'd have had somebody who was the examiner, then that was kind of a feather in his cap.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: And so I -- I guess -- they'd always told me you have to ask, they don't ask you. Well, in this case, somehow, they asked me, and I think it was because -- I think like most businesses, most employers needed to have a minority. Well, okay, the General Aviation district office in Sacramento which headed everything in that part of the country needed a minority, and I -- I guess they decided I would do fine. So I started with the FAA in '7 -- let's see, it was probably '74, and I stayed there for the next ten years, and it just got -- I -- I liked it, but they had gotten so extreme on what they wanted an examiner to do that you just couldn't -- you couldn't pass a single person. There's no way anybody could pass. It said you have to do this, you have to do that, and you didn't say, like you used to, you may. But anyway, I resigned from that and just became -- just a flight instructor again, but we did get one of my fella 99's, another instructor, the job of examiner in my place, so we kind of kept it for the women.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Oh, that's great. And do you want to spend just a minute talking about what the 99's are?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Sure will, get a drink of water.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Sure.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Okay. The 99's is an international association of women pilots, and it started in 1929 with 99 women. They had sent notices to every licensed woman pilot in those days, and they got 99 people who were interested, and that's why it's called the 99. Amelia Earhart was the first president. So it started out pretty nice, and I had heard of it, but in Rialto, I didn't know anybody that was a 99, and then when my -- when I flew the ftrst derby, it was sponsored by the 1899's, and I thought gee, you know, if they do this kind of a thing, it's worth belonging to, and nobody even asked me to join. I thought they had made a mistake, they ought to get all these new people out, but they didn't. So when I got back into Rialto and I started asking, the closest chapter was in San Gabriel about 30 miles west, so I -- I joined that chapter, and eventually -- gee whiz, I joined the I chapter back in Washington when I was back there. I joined another one when they had enough girls to form a chapter in Riverside area --

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: -- and then when I moved to Redding, one of the women was - wanted to start a chapter, so we got together and we started a chapter up there, and it's still in operation, called the Mt. Shasta chapter, and it has just grown. It's now -- there are 3,000, I think, members in the north -- I'm sorry, the southwestern chapter which takes in California, Arizona, Nevada, I believe, yeah.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Hm-hmm.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Well, that's great. Well, is there anything else you want to add before we end the interview; is there anything you can think of?

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: No, except I appreciate it. As I say, I've always felt guilty 'cause I had such a good time during the war, and I just -- I still feel guilty.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Well, we thank you very much for your time.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: Well, I thank you so much. I just hope this is -- well, I know it's going to be filed away and nobody probably ever see it anyway.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Ob, I think they will.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: I don't know.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: But I hope it's okay. I didn't practice.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Thank you.

sp.speaker: Jane A. La Mar
sp.p: I just sat down and did it.

sp.speaker: Caroline N. Mitchell
sp.p: Yep, that's great. Okay.
